title: Monolith versus microservices

definition.text: The choice between building an application as one deployable unit or as many small independent services, which depends on team, business maturity and latency needs.

facts.text: Singh's guide advises starting with a monolith when building a new system, while accepting that each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages.
Microservices are not a silver bullet; they solve an organizational problem, and adopting them is about organizational priorities and team structure as much as technology.
Questions to ask before moving to microservices include whether the team is too large for a shared codebase, whether teams are blocked on other teams, and whether they bring clear business value.
Further questions are whether the business is mature enough and whether the current architecture limits the team through communication overhead.
Not every application must be broken into microservices; they are solutions to complex concerns, and a business without such concerns does not need them.

Latency-sensitive applications such as real-time gaming, at milli-second latency, and low-latency trading, at micro-second latency, avoid microservices because network latency between separate processes is unbearable.
Microservices are usually stateless, with state kept in a database, but real-time gaming and trading keep state in memory for quick updates.
These applications also talk to the server at high frequency and must reach the same running instance, so they need web socket connections and sticky routing.

contested_note: Whether to begin with a monolith or microservices depends on team size, business maturity and latency needs.
notes: Singh's advice to start with a monolith is the guide's own recommendation.

definition.text: A set of working rules for microservices: model them on the business domain, give each its own data, keep couplings loose and plan for failure.

facts.text: Model services around the business domain, with loose coupling and high functional cohesion, and make each microservice do one thing well.
Each service owns and manages its own data, kept private to it, so that coupling falls and services can evolve independently; shared database schemas are a cause of coupling.
Services should communicate only through well-designed APIs, avoid leaking implementation details, and keep API changes backward compatible.
Services should talk over lightweight protocols; options include REST, gRPC or message brokers.
Design for failure at infrastructure, database and service levels, using circuit breakers, bulkheads or graceful degradation, and fail fast so failures do not cascade.
Resiliency patterns such as retry policies, caching and rate limiting improve the availability of the services.
A large attack surface calls for security at every level of the communication path, and with many services centralized logging becomes critical for finding issues.
Containerization with tools like Docker and Kubernetes deploys microservices in isolation and simplifies their scaling and deployment.

definition.text: Common mistakes that make a microservices architecture fail to deliver its promised benefits.

facts.text: Service boundaries not drawn around the business domain, a lack of business alignment and a lack of clear ownership are common pitfalls.
Teams underestimate how hard it is to build a distributed system, and a lack of design for fault tolerance can cause cascading failures.
A shared database or common dependencies between services undermines their independence.
A lack of idempotency and trying to do everything ACID instead of BASE are further pitfalls.

definition.text: A system that looks like microservices but is tightly coupled internally, like a monolithic application.

facts.text: A distributed monolith resembles the microservices architecture but is tightly coupled within itself like a monolithic application.
Signs are a need for low-latency communication, services that do not scale easily, dependencies between services, shared resources such as databases, and tightly coupled systems.
Scalability is a primary reason to adopt microservices, but a distributed monolith makes most components depend on one another, which increases design complexity.

definition.text: A single deployed application whose code is split into independent modules, one per feature.

facts.text: A modular monolith builds and deploys a single application but breaks the code into independent modules for each feature.
Reducing each module's dependencies lets a module be enhanced or changed without affecting other modules.
Done right, it reduces the complexity of maintaining a monolith as the system grows, which pays off in the long term.

definition.text: Two ways microservices collaborate: through shared rules for exchanging messages (choreography) or through a central coordinator that calls and combines the services (orchestration).

facts.text: Service choreography describes the exchange of messages and the rules by which the microservices interact, with point-to-point communication between them.
In orchestration, the orchestrator acts as a center of authority responsible for invoking and combining the services, and it describes the interactions between all participating services.
The orchestration pattern also includes transaction management among different services.

Orchestration is more reliable because it has built-in transaction management and error handling, while choreography's point-to-point communication makes fault tolerance scenarios much more complicated.
Orchestration scales more easily in one respect: adding a service means only the orchestrator changes its interaction rules, whereas in choreography all the interacting services must change.
Orchestration adds latency because all services talk through a central orchestrator, and throughput is bound to the orchestrator's capacity.
The orchestrator is a single point of failure, since if it goes down no services can talk to each other, so it must be highly available.
Netflix Conductor is a real-world microservice orchestrator.

definition.text: The usual building blocks around a set of microservices: a load balancer, CDN, API gateway, identity provider, service registry, management component and domain services with their own databases.

facts.text: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend services, and a CDN, a group of geographically distributed servers holding static content, is checked first by clients before they reach the backend.
The API gateway handles incoming requests and routes them to the relevant services, talking to the identity provider and to service discovery.
The identity provider handles authentication and authorization for users.
Services register themselves in the service registry and discovery component, which the API gateway searches to find the services it needs to talk to.
A management component monitors the services.
Microservices are designed and deployed in different domains, and each domain has its own database.

definition.text: An architecture that divides an application into logical layers, each with a specific responsibility, which may run on physically separate tiers.

facts.text: Layers separate responsibilities and manage dependencies: a higher layer can use services in a lower layer but not the other way around.
Tiers are physically separated and run on separate machines; a tier can call another directly or use asynchronous messaging, and several layers may share one tier.
Physically separating tiers improves scalability and resiliency but adds latency from the extra network communication.
In a closed layer architecture a layer can only call the next layer down, which limits dependencies but may create unnecessary network traffic; in an open one it can call any layer below.
The widely used 3-tier design has a presentation layer for user interactions, a business logic layer that validates data, and a data access layer that operates on the database.
In 2-tier, the presentation layer runs on the client and talks to a data store with no business logic layer; in single-tier, everything runs on one application or server.
Advantages are improved availability, firewall-like layers for security, independent scaling of tiers and easier maintenance by different people.
Disadvantages are added complexity, network latency that grows with the number of tiers, a hardware cost per tier, and harder network security.

definition.text: The two main service discovery patterns: the client queries a service registry itself, or it calls a load balancer that finds an instance for it.

facts.text: In client-side discovery, one of two main patterns, the client obtains a service's location by querying a service registry that manages and stores the network locations of all services.
In server-side discovery, the client sends its request to an intermediate component such as a load balancer, which forwards it to an available service instance.
Tools used to implement service discovery include Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes Services and Apache Zookeeper.

definition.text: A highly available database of the network locations of service instances, kept current by services registering themselves or by a third party doing it for them.

facts.text: A service registry is a database containing the network locations of service instances that clients can reach, and it must be highly available and up to date.
With self-registration, a service instance registers and de-registers itself in the registry.
A self-registered instance may also send heartbeat requests to keep its registration alive.

With third-party registration, the registry tracks running instances by polling the deployment environment or subscribing to events, records newly available instances and de-registers terminated ones.

definition.text: An architecture that organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols and can be deployed and scaled independently.

facts.text: A microservice architecture organizes an application into loosely coupled, fine-grained services that communicate through lightweight protocols, which teams can develop, deploy and scale independently.
There is no universally agreed definition, but each service is generally designed around one business capability within a bounded context, with its own codebase managed by a small team.
Each service persists its own data, a database per service, unlike the traditional model where a separate data layer handles persistence.
Typical characteristics are loose coupling, small but focused scope (a matter of responsibility, not size), organization around business capabilities, resilience to failure, and high maintainability.
Services can be deployed independently, give multiple teams agility, improve fault tolerance and data isolation, and remove any long-term commitment to a particular technology stack.

Services scale independently: a monolith supporting three functions must be scaled in its entirety even if only one is constrained, whereas with microservices only that function's service is scaled out.

Costs include the complexity of a distributed system, harder testing, expensive maintenance, challenging inter-service communication, data integrity and consistency problems, and network latency and congestion.

The complexity of a monolith does not disappear when it is split into services; some becomes operational complexity, so decentralized continuous delivery and DevOps with holistic monitoring are needed.

definition.text: How big or small to make each service, a trade-off between independence and the cost of communication between services.

facts.text: The right granularity is found through iterative collaboration between architects and developers, weighing user requirements, service responsibilities and non-functional requirements, and is ultimately set by business drivers.

Neal Ford's integrator factors, such as shared transactions or tightly coupled processes, favor combining services, while disintegrator factors, such as fault tolerance or independent scalability, favor splitting them.
Very fine-grained services are easier to test and deploy independently but tend to have lower performance and reliability because of more interservice communication and more complex choreography.
Coarse-grained services are more robust and reliable thanks to less communication overhead and coordination complexity, but are harder to test and deploy because a change affects a wider scope.

definition.text: A natural division of business logic with an explicit boundary inside which one domain model is consistent and valid.

facts.text: A bounded context, a core idea of domain-driven design, defines an area within which a domain model is consistent and valid, ensuring clarity and separation of concerns.
A bounded context often maps to a microservice, and a one-to-one mapping is typically ideal because it keeps clear boundaries, reduces coupling and enables independent deployment and scaling.
One context may be split into several microservices for varying scalability needs, or several contexts consolidated into one microservice for simplicity or lower operational overhead.
The choice should balance domain-driven design principles with business goals, technical constraints and operational requirements.

definition.text: A design that organizes resources into self-contained cells, each running a set of microservices and serving part of the requests, to limit the blast radius of failures.

facts.text: Cell-based architecture organizes computational resources into self-contained cells, each operating independently on a subset of requests while keeping scalability, fault isolation and availability.
A cell typically holds multiple microservices and acts as an autonomous unit.
Entire sets of microservices may be replicated across cells so requests can be rerouted to another operational cell on failure, limiting the impact of localized failures.
Circuit breakers within a cell mitigate cascading failures among microservices, while inter-cell circuit breakers isolate failing cells and redirect traffic to the remaining ones.

definition.text: Replacing parts of a monolith with microservices step by step, moving application code first and decoupling the data later.

facts.text: Microservices are considered a viable way to modernize an existing monolith, and modernization of legacy applications is done incrementally.
The data-driven migration antipattern is prioritizing data migration during the move from a monolith to microservices.
An iterative approach migrates application code first, with new microservices temporarily relying on the existing monolithic database.
As the system becomes better understood, data is decoupled and restructured so each microservice has its own database, which simplifies migration and reduces data migration errors.

definition.text: Reporting by pulling data straight out of each microservice's store, which breaks bounded contexts or delivers stale data.

facts.text: Retrieving data for a reporting service can break the bounded contexts of microservices, reduce the timeliness of the data, or both.
This holds whether data is pulled directly from databases, retrieved via HTTP, or collected in batches, and the pattern is called the reach-in reporting antipattern.
An alternative is for the databases to asynchronously push the needed data to the reporting service instead of it pulling the data.
Pushing needs a separate contract between the microservices and the reporting service and can be complex, but it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

definition.text: Ways to deal with the need to share code across services in an architecture that ideally shares nothing.

facts.text: Ideally microservices follow a share-nothing architecture, but in practice code must often be shared across services.

Common approaches are separate shared libraries for reusable components such as a security library, replicating stable modules with minimal changes across services, or consolidating several microservices into one.
Each approach has its own advantages and trade-offs depending on context and requirements.

definition.text: Practices that keep many independently deployed services testable and visible: stable interfaces, contract tests and aggregated logs, metrics and traces.

facts.text: Sam Newman suggests keeping microservice interfaces stable and making backwards-compatible changes as they evolve, so deployments need not be coordinated across services.
Newman proposes consumer-driven contract testing as a better alternative to traditional end-to-end testing for microservices.
He also suggests log aggregation, metrics aggregation and distributed tracing tools to keep systems of microservices observable.
Richards and Ford propose that each microservice have its own architectural characteristics rather than uniform ones for the whole distributed system.

definition.text: A single, self-contained application designed as one service that performs every step needed for a business function.

facts.text: A monolith is built as a single unit and handles every step needed to satisfy a business need, rather than one particular task.
Advantages are simple development and debugging, fast and reliable communication, easy monitoring and testing, and support for ACID transactions.
Monoliths are relatively simple and low cost, but they lack elasticity, fault tolerance and scalability.
Maintenance gets harder as the codebase grows, the application is tightly coupled and hard to extend, and it commits the team to a particular technology stack.
The whole application is redeployed on each update, a single bug can bring down the entire system, and scaling or adopting new technologies is difficult.
A monolith is still a good choice for a small team and little complexity; once it becomes too complex, it can be refactored into microservices or a distributed application.
On a single machine a monolith may be performant enough for the current workload, yet it is less available, durable, changeable, fine-tuned and scalable than a well-designed distributed system.
Common architectural patterns for monoliths, each with trade-offs, are layered architecture, modular monolith and microkernel architecture.

definition.text: The process of automatically detecting services on a network, so clients can find service instances whose locations change.

facts.text: Service discovery automatically detects devices and services on a network, aiming to reduce the manual configuration effort required from users and administrators.
In a monolith, services invoke one another through language-level method or procedure calls.

Microservices run in virtualized or containerized environments where the number and location of service instances change dynamically, so clients need a mechanism to reach a changing set of ephemeral instances.

A service discovery protocol is a network protocol that helps accomplish discovery, and discovery needs a common language so software agents can use one another's services without continuous user intervention.
Many protocols exist, including DNS Service Discovery, Simple Service Discovery Protocol, and DNS as used in Kubernetes.
Kubernetes provides two modes of service discovery, using environment variables or Kubernetes DNS.

definition.text: A dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication using a proxy paired with each service.

facts.text: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication that gives observability into communications, secure connections, and automated retries and backoff for failed requests.
Routing service-to-service communication becomes increasingly complex as the number of services grows, and a service mesh makes it managed, observable and secure.
It consists of network proxies paired with each service, called the data plane, and a set of management processes, called the control plane.
The data plane intercepts and processes calls between services, while the control plane coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.
Each service instance is paired with a reverse proxy called a sidecar, sharing its container, with containers managed by an orchestration tool such as Kubernetes.
The sidecars can support service discovery, load balancing, authentication and authorization, and secure communications, and the mesh works with a service discovery protocol to detect services.
Istio, Cilium, Linkerd and Consul implement the architecture, and many meshes use the Envoy proxy on the data plane.

definition.text: An architectural style built from discrete services, each a unit of functionality that can be accessed remotely and updated independently, instead of one monolithic design.

facts.text: SOA focuses on discrete services instead of a monolithic design, is intended to be independent of vendors, products and technologies, and is a good choice for system integration.

One definition gives a service four properties: it represents a repeatable business activity with a specified outcome, is self-contained, is a black box to its consumers, and may be composed of other services.

Services and consumers communicate by passing data in a well-defined, shared format or by coordinating an activity between services, and the aim is to build applications purely from existing services.
SOA promotes reuse at the macro (service) level rather than the class level, and can simplify interconnection to and use of existing legacy assets.

Treating a service as a project separate from its consumers lets it be delivered quickly and independently, and encourages good design because the service is designed without knowing who its consumers are.
SOA can be implemented with web services or microservices, commonly using web services standards such as SOAP, or with other service technologies such as REST or gRPC.

Without native or binary remote procedure call forms, applications could run more slowly and need more processing power, though SOA can be implemented with technologies that avoid RPC and XML or JSON translation.
Stateful services reduce the provider's scalability if it must keep each consumer's context and increase coupling, and testing is hard because of the lack of a uniform testing framework.

definition.text: A set of published guidelines for designing services that stay loosely coupled, reusable and independent of their consumers.

facts.text: There are no industry standards for the exact composition of a service-oriented architecture, though many industry sources have published their own principles.

Services adhere to a standardized service contract and stay loosely coupled through reference autonomy, where services only know of each other's existence, and location transparency, where a service can be called from anywhere in the network.
Services act as black boxes that hide their inner logic, are autonomous over the functionality they encapsulate, and are stateless, returning a value or an exception to minimize resource use.
Services should be long lived, composable into other services, discoverable through communicative metadata, and divided to promote reuse of code.

definition.text: The three roles in SOA: a provider publishes a service, a broker makes it findable, and a consumer finds and binds to it.

facts.text: Each SOA building block can play any of three roles: service provider, service broker (also called registry or repository), or service requester (consumer).
The provider creates a web service and provides its information to the service registry.
The broker makes information about the service available to any potential requester; public brokers are available everywhere while private brokers reach a limited public.

A consumer locates entries in the broker registry with find operations and then binds to the provider to invoke its web services, under a standardized service contract with business, functional and technical parts.

title: Microservices versus SOA

definition.text: How microservices relate to service-oriented architecture: sometimes used interchangeably, but differing in scope and aim.

facts.text: Microservices and SOA are sometimes used interchangeably, but they differ, and the main distinction comes down to scope.

SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards, whereas microservices are many smallest independent service units aimed at team autonomy and decoupling.
Another view calls microservices a modern interpretation of SOA, a new implementation approach popular since 2014 that stresses continuous deployment and agile practices.

Characteristics of microservices found in the literature include fine-grained interfaces, business-driven development, polyglot programming and persistence, lightweight container deployment, decentralized continuous delivery and DevOps with holistic service monitoring.

notes: The two framings define the terms differently (Singh: distinct approaches; Wikipedia SOA article: microservices are a realisation of SOA), so both are stated as views, not as a conflict.
